Higher
hī'-ēr
adj. (comparative of high: greater in elevation, in authority, or in kind)
Comparative of high, Saxon heah. The Authorized Version uses higher in three registers that the reader should keep distinct: physical stature, delegated authority, and the incommensurable difference between God and man.

Biblical Definition

Higher measures three different things in Scripture, and confusing them is a doctrinal error rather than a reading error. It measures stature: Saul “was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward” (1Sa 9:2) — and the man Israel chose by the eye was the man who failed. It measures office: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1), where the magistrate is genuinely above the citizen and yet is himself ordained of God, so that his height is borrowed and answerable. And it measures the distance between the Creator and the creature: “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts” (Isa 55:9). That last is not a difference of degree along one scale; it is the whole reason revelation is necessary. A God whose thoughts were higher by measurement could be reached by climbing. A God whose thoughts are higher as the heavens are higher than the earth must come down or remain unknown. Hence the prayer of the man who has stopped climbing: “lead me to the rock that is higher than I” (Psa 61:2). The refuge is above him, and he asks to be led to it rather than boasting that he has found it. And of Messiah the Father says, “I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” (Psa 89:27) — the one height that is His by right and not by grant.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines high as elevated, lofty, and figuratively as exalted in rank, condition or excellence; higher as its comparative degree.

expand to see more

HIGH, a. Extending to a great distance above the surface of the earth; elevated; lofty; of great altitude.

1. Elevated in rank, condition or office; as a high official; the higher powers.

2. Exalted in excellence or extent; as the high attributes of the Deity.

3. Proud; haughty; lofty in an ill sense; as a high look.

Key Scripture

Isa 55:9 — "For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts."

Psa 61:2 — "From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I."

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

Psa 89:27 — "Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."

Modern Corruption

“A higher power” has been emptied into a nameless something; Scripture names Him and names His ways.

expand to see more

The phrase a higher power now circulates as a deliberately unnamed abstraction — a something above me, of no particular character, to which nothing in particular is owed. Scripture never speaks this way. The higher powers of Romans 13 are concrete magistrates with a sword and an account to render; the One whose ways are higher in Isaiah 55 has a name, a covenant, and a summons two verses earlier: let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return unto the LORD. Height in Isaiah is the ground of a call to repent, not a reason to keep the deity vague.

The other corruption runs the opposite way: the assumption that God's higher ways make His revealed word uncertain, so that any hard text may be set aside as unknowable. That reverses the passage. Isaiah says God's thoughts are higher and therefore His word is to be trusted where it speaks — the very next verses promise that the word that goeth forth out of His mouth shall not return void. Transcendence is the guarantee of Scripture's authority, never an excuse for evading it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gabahh (H1361), to be high, exalted; rum (H7311), to be lifted up; Greek huperecho (G5242), to hold above, to be superior.

expand to see more

Hebrew gabahh (H1361) — to be high, tall, lofty; Isaiah 55:9, of the heavens above the earth.

Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to rise, to be lifted up; used both of God's exaltation and of the proud heart lifted up.

Hebrew tsur (H6697) — rock; Psalm 61:2, the rock that is higher than I.

Greek huperecho (G5242) — to have or hold above, to excel, to be superior; Romans 13:1 (higher powers), Philippians 2:3, 4:7.

Greek hupsistos (G5310) — highest, most high; Luke 2:14, Hebrews 7:1.

Usage

"“Higher than any of the people” — and Israel chose by the eye."

"“The rock that is higher than I” — a man who has stopped climbing."

"“So are my ways higher than your ways” — the reason revelation exists."
